blocks.text: There are many proofs of the stellio's skill. Hesychius, under Κωλώτης [Kōlōtēs], says that the stellio εὐστόχως ἅλλεσθαι περὶ τὰς μυίας [eustochōs hallesthai peri tas myias], leaps skilfully about flies; that is, in order to catch them. Phavorinus ineptly has περὶ τοὺς μῦς [peri tous mys], about mice: with which the stellio has nothing to do. But Augustine also speaks of flies in book 10 of the Confessions, chapter 35: What of it, when, as I sit at home, a stellio catching flies, or a spider entangling them as they rush into its webs, often holds my attention? Theophrastus, in the book De anim. invid., adduces another proof, but a less certain one: Ὅτι ὁ γαλεώτης, φθονῶν τῆς ὠφελείας τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, καταπίνει τὸ δέρμα, ὅταν ἐκδύηται· ἔστι γὰρ βοήθημα ἐπιλήπτῳ· [Hoti ho galeōtēs, phthonōn tēs ōpheleias tois anthrōpois, katapinei to derma, hotan ekdyētai; esti gar boēthēma epilēptō;] The stellio, begrudging men the benefit, devours its own skin as soon as it has shed it. For it helps those suffering from epilepsy. Antigonus has the same in the Mirabilia, chapter 24, and Apuleius in his first Apology for himself. And from this Pliny, book 30, chapter 10, concludes that no animal more deceitfully begrudges man. From the same source the names stelliones [swindlers] and stellionatus [fraud] were transferred into terms of abuse. There are also those who think that the Galeotae, the most skilful interpreters of portents in Sicily, took their name from the cleverness of this animal. To this Stephanus refers these words: Γαλεῶται μάντεων εἶδος Σικελῶν· Γαλεὸς δὲ, ὁ ἀσκαλαβώτης [Galeōtai manteōn eidos Sikelōn; Galeos de, ho askalabōtēs] (where for γαλεὸς [galeos] one should read γαλεώτης [galeōtēs]). But since in Hebrew גלה gala means to reveal, which is most characteristic of seers, I suspect that the name of the Galeotae is Hebrew, like a great many others which, as I have proved elsewhere, were carried over into Sicily with the colonies of the Phoenicians.

But Solomon himself amply proves the stellio's skill with these words: It takes hold with its hands, and is in kings' palaces. Why he attributes hands to it is obscure to no one. Just as lacertus [lizard] is named from lacerti, that is, arms, so the stellio is called in Greek κωλώτης [kōlōtēs] from τοῖς κώλοις [tois kōlois]. Κῶλα [Kōla] are hands and feet. I call the forefeet hands together with Avicenna ^{e)}, who writes that غظاية [ghaẓāya] adhajam, that is, the salamander (in Avicenna's view), is preserved in honey only if it is gutted and يداها ورجلاها [yadāhā wa-rijlāhā] its hands and feet are cut off: where Dioscorides has φυλάσσεται ἐν μέλιτι ἐξεντεριθεῖσα, τῶν ποδῶν ἀφαιρεθέντων [phylassetai en meliti exenteritheisa, tōn podōn aphairethentōn]. If the salamander has hands, why not also the stellio, an animal very like the salamander? Thus Damir, in the chapter حردون [ḥardūn] Chardaun, or On the land crocodile: له كف ككف الانسان مقسومة الاصابع الا انامل [lahu kaff ka-kaff al-insān maqsūmat al-aṣābiʿ illā anāmil] It has a hand like the hand of a man, with fingers divided into joints. Indeed, you may rightly call the feet of any lizard, especially [II, 518] the forefeet, hands, since they are like hands. Gesner, from his own observation: The lacertus is named from its likeness to the lacerti [arms] of a man, because their feet [col. 1089] are likewise split into fingers, as if from hollow hands or palms. The same: Very slender fingers, five in front and five behind, with little claws. On the hind feet the longest is the one that occupies the place of the index finger; the thumb is in a lower position, as in the hands of man: but the front feet have the thumb in the same position as the other fingers. You see that the forefeet, or more truly the arms, are in the shape of a human arm and hand, with the same number of fingers, and in the same position. How much better does the name hands suit such arms than the legs of spiders?
